transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, so, I guess what really brought me in is... well, it’s my work, mostly. I’m a jeweler, I work with precious metals, custom pieces, sizing, that kind of thing. I've been doing it since right out of high school, and it takes a lot of focus, right? You’re working with a jeweler's saw or a micro-torch, and you have to be completely locked in. 

But lately, what really brought me in is that my mind just absolutely will not stay on one thing anymore. It's like a TV changing channels on its own. I'll be sitting at the bench, getting ready to file something down, and suddenly I’m thinking about a customer email I need to reply to. So I stop to think about that, but then I notice a tiny saw mark on a piece of scrap metal on my desk, and I start wondering how that got there and if my blades are getting dull. Then I hear a noise outside—like a car door slamming or a dog barking across the street—and I'm instantly looking out the window trying to figure out what’s going on. 

And then I look back at my desk and I realize I’ve completely lost the whole work order. Like, the actual slip of paper is buried somewhere, or I just have absolutely no idea whose piece I'm even holding anymore or what I was supposed to be doing to it. It’s just happening constantly, every single day, and I can't afford to be making mistakes with materials this expensive, you know? I try to sit down and just power through it, but five seconds later I'm distracted by the dust floating in the light from my desk lamp. It's just really starting to mess everything up, and I don't know how to turn it off.
How long have you been experiencing this difficulty with your thoughts jumping around and getting distracted so easily?

Well, so, it’s kind of a specific timeline, actually. Um, because I can pinpoint exactly when it started getting really bad. See, there was this big jewelry show downtown, the annual one—it's a huge deal for local artisans, right? You spend months prepping for it, making sure your display is perfect, making sure your best pieces are polished to a mirror finish. And, well, I actually won an award there this year. Best in Show for Custom Design. It was this incredible feeling, you know? Just validation for all those years at the bench since high school. 

But right after that, right after they handed me the plaque and the weekend wrapped up, that’s when this whole wired, out-of-control stretch really kicked into high gear. I mean, I came back to my shop on Monday, and instead of just getting back to the grind, my brain was just... vibrating. And that specific feeling, that absolute inability to hold a thought for more than a second without it ricocheting off the walls? That went on for about two weeks straight. Just fourteen days of pure, unadulterated mental pinball. I remember looking at the calendar, trying to track when I was supposed to ship out orders, and realizing two whole weeks had passed where I was just buzzing out of my skin and getting absolutely nothing finished. So yeah, about two weeks of that really intense, jumpy phase right after the show.

During those two weeks after the jewelry show when your thoughts were jumping around and you felt mentally 'vibrating' or 'buzzing out of your skin,' did you also feel unusually high, elated, or maybe even irritable, like you had extra energy or needed less sleep?

Yeah, oh man, it was... it was exactly like that. I mean, right after they called my name for the Best in Show, it was like someone flipped a switch in my chest. I just felt... lit up. Completely electrified. Like I was suddenly larger than life, you know? I remember walking back to my booth and feeling like I was floating, like I could literally do anything. I was telling everyone I was going to open a flagship store in New York, that I was going to revolutionize custom casting techniques. I just felt so incredibly good, so high on life, like every idea I had was absolute gold and nobody could touch me. 

But then, at the same time, if anyone tried to bring me down to earth, I would just snap. Like, my business partner, he was trying to get me to focus on the regular shop hours, telling me we needed to stick to the schedule, and I just lost it on him. I was so irritable, so quick to anger. I remember yelling at him, telling him he was small-minded, that he was trying to anchor me down when I was ready to fly. If anyone asked me to slow down or be practical, it was like they were speaking a foreign language and I just had zero patience for it. I was so amped up, so full of this intense energy, that any kind of restriction just made me furious. So yeah, it was this crazy mix of feeling like a god one second and then wanting to bite someone's head off the next if they got in my way.
Did there come a point when your mood was not just high or irritable for a few hours or part of the day, but was like that most of the day, nearly every day, for at least a full week?

Yeah, exactly. I mean, it wasn't just a mood swing or, like, having a good morning and then crashing after lunch. It was relentless. Like I said before, that whole wired, out-of-control stretch started literally the moment they handed me that award at the jewelry show, and it didn't let up. It went on for about two weeks straight. 

And when I say straight, I mean it was every single day, from the second I opened my eyes—which was usually way too early, anyway—until I finally managed to force myself to lay down at night. Most of the day, nearly every day, for those entire fourteen days. I remember waking up on a Tuesday, four days after the show, and I was already buzzing before my feet even hit the floor. I was already planning out six different custom rings in my head, feeling like I was on top of the world, and then by noon I was snapping at the mailman because he didn't hand me the packages fast enough. It was just this constant, humming baseline of either being incredibly high or incredibly irritable, all day long. It never really turned off during that whole two-week period. It was just... exhausting, looking back on it, but at the time, I just couldn't stop.
Did this high or irritated mood happen every day during that two-week period, and was it present most of the day each day?

Yeah, I mean, I know I just said it, but yes, absolutely. Every single day. Like I was saying, that whole wired, totally out-of-control stretch, it started literally right after they handed me that Best in Show award at the jewelry show. Like, the exact moment the weekend wrapped up and I walked out of that convention center, the clock started ticking on it. And it went on for about two weeks straight. Fourteen days of just... constant, nonstop buzzing. 

It wasn't like it faded in and out, you know? It wasn't like, oh, I feel great on Monday, but Tuesday I'm back to normal. It was present most of the day, every day, for that entire two-week block. I remember trying to sit at my workbench—I have this really nice antique jeweler's bench I restored myself, solid oak, beautiful piece of furniture—and I'd sit there at 8 AM, already feeling like I'd drank ten cups of coffee, and that feeling would just ride with me until the sun went down and beyond. So, yeah, to answer your question, it was every day, most of the day, for about two weeks straight right after that show.
Would you say that during that two-week period, your mood was not only high or irritable but also clearly different from your usual self, and that this change was noticeable to others around you?

Oh, man, night and day. Absolutely night and day. I mean, anyone who knows me knows I'm usually pretty meticulous, right? You kind of have to be when you're working with precious metals and stones—you can't just wing it. But during those two weeks... yeah, I was a totally different person, and everybody saw it. It was impossible to miss. 

Like, just to give you an idea of how off the rails I went, I completely missed a major custom delivery. It was supposed to be this intricate platinum engagement ring with a custom bezel setting for a client who’s been coming to me since I first started out in my garage. But I was just so caught up in all my grand ideas and buzzing around the shop that I just... I blew right past the deadline. Didn't even realize it until they called. And my shop records? Usually, I have this whole system, everything tracked and filed, but it got so incredibly disorganized—just invoices and sketches and half-finished wax molds piled everywhere—that I literally had to put a freeze on everything. I had to stop taking new work for now just to untangle the mess I made of my own business. 

And it wasn't just work, either. My family, they've been hovering like crazy lately. My mom and my sister started calling and dropping by the shop way more than they ever do. They got really worried because they saw how far I’d slipped from my usual routines. Like, I usually do Sunday dinners with them, and I was just blowing them off, or I'd answer the phone and just talk a mile a minute about my flagship store idea without letting them get a word in. They could tell just by looking at me and seeing the absolute chaotic state of my workbench that I wasn't myself. So they’ve been checking on me constantly now. It's actually been kind of suffocating, to be honest, having them text me all the time to see if I'm eating or working, but... I guess I can't really blame them when I look back at the disaster I made of my ledger and my schedule.

After that two-week period of feeling high, irritable, and distracted, did you experience a period where you felt down, depressed, or hopeless for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Well, yeah, it's like a switch flipped. You know, I was flying so high, buzzing around my workbench, and then... it just stopped. And these past couple weeks, it's been the exact opposite. It's like I wake up, and there's just this heavy, hollow feeling sitting right in my chest. You know when you polish a piece of silver and it gets that beautiful, mirror-like finish, but then it tarnishes and just looks dull and gray? That's exactly how everything feels right now. Like the shine has just completely gone out of everything in my life. 

It's been most of the day, every single day, for a solid two weeks now. I mean, I drag myself out of bed, but it's a monumental effort. And I'll drive to the shop—my shop is just this little storefront down on Elm, nothing fancy, but it's mine, you know? I usually love pulling up to it, seeing my name on the window. But lately, I'll park my truck out back by the alley, and I just... I can't bring myself to get out. I've literally just sat there in the driver's seat, staring at the steering wheel, and I've just started crying. Crying in my truck before I even unlock the back door to open the shop. And it's not even like there's a specific reason I'm crying, it's just this overwhelming sense of... nothingness. 

And then I get inside, and I look at all the mess I made during those two weeks I was wired, all the half-finished molds and the disorganized ledger, and it just makes that heavy feeling worse. I sit at my oak bench, and I just stare at my tools. My favorite engraving gravers, my jewelers saw... I just look at them and feel completely hopeless. Like, what's the point? I don't want to touch them. I don't want to talk to clients. I just want to put my head down on the bench and disappear. So, yeah, it's been really bad these last two weeks. Just a constant, heavy, miserable feeling all day long.

During that two-week period when you felt so high and irritable, did you also experience a decreased need for sleep, talk more rapidly than usual, feel like your thoughts were racing, or become more involved in risky or pleasurable activities without considering the consequences?

Oh, man, the sleep... or, I guess, the total lack of sleep. Yeah, that was definitely a huge part of it. It’s funny you ask that, because usually, I'm the kind of guy who needs a solid eight hours. If I don't get my eight hours, my hands get a little shaky, and you really can't have shaky hands when you're setting a two-carat diamond into a custom platinum prong, you know? But during those two weeks, right after that jewelry show? It was like my body just completely forgot how to be tired. 

I would lay down at maybe midnight, right? And I'd just lay there, staring at the ceiling, thinking about all these massive ideas I had for the shop. And then, boom, by 2:00 or 3:00 in the morning, my eyes would just snap open. And I wasn't groggy. I wasn't dragging. I felt completely, 100% clear-headed. Like I had just slept for twelve hours and drank a pot of coffee. I’d be so incredibly excited, just buzzing with energy, that I’d literally jump out of bed. 

I’d head straight down to the shop—sometimes it was still pitch black outside, not even a hint of sunrise—and I'd just start working. I’d be cutting stones, sketching out these wild, elaborate new designs, taking photos of my workbench and posting them all over my social media pages, talking about how I was going to revolutionize the custom jewelry market in our city. I mean, two or three hours of sleep, max, and I felt like Superman. It was wild. My mind was just going a million miles a minute, and I just couldn't turn it off. I didn't even want to turn it off, to be honest. I felt like I was wasting time if I was sleeping.

During that two-week period when you felt so high and irritable, did you find yourself doing things much more quickly or intensely than usual, like rushing around the shop constantly or working at a speed that was hard to keep up with?

Oh, absolutely. It was like I had a motor running inside me that just wouldn't shut off, and the gas pedal was glued to the floor. I mean, usually, jewelry work is all about patience, right? It's a very stationary job. You sit at your bench, you get your loupe on your eye, you brace your arms, and you breathe slow so your hands stay perfectly steady. It's very focused. 

But during those two weeks? I literally couldn't sit still at the bench. I physically could not do it. I would sit down, grab my pencil, and I'd bounce from sketching this crazy new watch case—which, by the way, I don't even normally do watches, I'm mostly rings and pendants, but suddenly I was obsessed with this exposed-gear, rose-gold mechanical watch casing concept. I had all these ideas for the bezel and the lugs, just drawing furiously. But then, before I even finished the sketch, I’d just pop up out of my chair like I was on springs. 

I'd run over to the computer in the back office—well, it's really more of a storage closet with a laptop on a filing cabinet—and I'd start rapid-fire emailing all my suppliers. I'm talking metal brokers in New York, gemstone dealers, just demanding bulk quotes for all these materials I didn't even have the money for yet. And then, right in the middle of typing an email to a diamond guy, I'd suddenly decide the front showroom wasn't visually striking enough. So I'd leave the laptop open, march out to the front, and start completely rearranging all the velvet display trays. I'd pull every single piece out, color-coordinate the sapphires and the rubies, angle the rings so the track lighting hit the facets perfectly... 

And I'd be doing all of this long after closing time. The "Closed" sign had been flipped for hours, the street outside would be completely dead, pitch black, and I'm just in there pacing and bouncing from the bench to the computer to the display cases, over and over again, moving at warp speed. I was just a blur. It felt like if I stopped moving or working for even a single second, I’d just explode out of my own skin.

Usually, I have this whole system, everything tracked and filed, but it got so incredibly disorganized—just invoices and sketches and half-finished wax molds piled everywhere—that I literally had to put a freeze on everything. I had to stop taking new work for now just to untangle the mess I made of my own business. 

And it wasn't just work, either. My family, they've been hovering like crazy lately. My mom and my sister started calling and dropping by the shop way more than they ever do. They got really worried because they saw how far I’d slipped from my usual routines. Like, I usually do Sunday dinners with them, and I was just blowing them off, or I'd answer the phone and just talk a mile a minute about my flagship store idea without letting them get a word in. They could tell just by looking at me and seeing the absolute chaotic state of my workbench that I wasn't myself. So they’ve been checking on me constantly now. It's actually been kind of suffocating, to be honest, having them text me all the time to see if I'm eating or working, but... I guess I can't really blame them when I look back at the disaster I made of my ledger and my schedule.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experienced a major depressive episode following the manic episode, which would differentiate between F31.3 (Bipolar I disorder, current manic episode) and F31.2 (Bipolar I disorder, current episode hypomanic).
doctor.question: After that two-week period of feeling high, irritable, and distracted, did you experience a period where you felt down, depressed, or hopeless for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: These past couple weeks, I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling, like the shine has gone out of everything, and I’ve cried in the truck before opening the shop.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient experienced a period of feeling down, depressed, or hopeless, which directly corresponds to the Depressed Mood symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, it's like a switch flipped. You know, I was flying so high, buzzing around my workbench, and then... it just stopped. And these past couple weeks, it's been the exact opposite. It's like I wake up, and there's just this heavy, hollow feeling sitting right in my chest. You know when you polish a piece of silver and it gets that beautiful, mirror-like finish, but then it tarnishes and just looks dull and gray? That's exactly how everything feels right now. Like the shine has just completely gone out of everything in my life. 

It's been most of the day, every single day, for a solid two weeks now. I mean, I drag myself out of bed, but it's a monumental effort. And I'll drive to the shop—my shop is just this little storefront down on Elm, nothing fancy, but it's mine, you know? I usually love pulling up to it, seeing my name on the window. But lately, I'll park my truck out back by the alley, and I just... I can't bring myself to get out. I've literally just sat there in the driver's seat, staring at the steering wheel, and I've just started crying. Crying in my truck before I even unlock the back door to open the shop. And it's not even like there's a specific reason I'm crying, it's just this overwhelming sense of... nothingness. 

And then I get inside, and I look at all the mess I made during those two weeks I was wired, all the half-finished molds and the disorganized ledger, and it just makes that heavy feeling worse. I sit at my oak bench, and I just stare at my tools. My favorite engraving gravers, my jewelers saw... I just look at them and feel completely hopeless. Like, what's the point? I don't want to touch them. I don't want to talk to clients. I just want to put my head down on the bench and disappear. So, yeah, it's been really bad these last two weeks. Just a constant, heavy, miserable feeling all day long.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experienced a full manic episode, including whether there was a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood lasting at least one week and associated symptoms such as inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, or excessive involvement in risky behavior.
doctor.question: During that two-week period when you felt so high and irritable, did you also experience a decreased need for sleep, talk more rapidly than usual, feel like your thoughts were racing, or become more involved in risky or pleasurable activities without considering the consequences?

target_item.name: Decreased_Sleep
target_item.manifestation: For a while I was sleeping maybe two or three hours, then getting up clear-headed and excited to start cutting stones or posting new designs before sunrise.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question specifically asks if the patient experienced a decreased need for sleep during the two-week period of elevated mood, which matches this symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, man, the sleep... or, I guess, the total lack of sleep. Yeah, that was definitely a huge part of it. It’s funny you ask that, because usually, I'm the kind of guy who needs a solid eight hours. If I don't get my eight hours, my hands get a little shaky, and you really can't have shaky hands when you're setting a two-carat diamond into a custom platinum prong, you know? But during those two weeks, right after that jewelry show? It was like my body just completely forgot how to be tired. 

I would lay down at maybe midnight, right? And I'd just lay there, staring at the ceiling, thinking about all these massive ideas I had for the shop. And then, boom, by 2:00 or 3:00 in the morning, my eyes would just snap open. And I wasn't groggy. I wasn't dragging. I felt completely, 100% clear-headed. Like I had just slept for twelve hours and drank a pot of coffee. I’d be so incredibly excited, just buzzing with energy, that I’d literally jump out of bed. 

I’d head straight down to the shop—sometimes it was still pitch black outside, not even a hint of sunrise—and I'd just start working. I’d be cutting stones, sketching out these wild, elaborate new designs, taking photos of my workbench and posting them all over my social media pages, talking about how I was going to revolutionize the custom jewelry market in our city. I mean, two or three hours of sleep, max, and I felt like Superman. It was wild. My mind was just going a million miles a minute, and I just couldn't turn it off. I didn't even want to turn it off, to be honest. I felt like I was wasting time if I was sleeping.

inference.note: The patient reported a distinct period of abnormally elevated and irritable mood lasting at least one week (clearly two weeks in this case), accompanied by decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, and increased goal-directed activity. This manic episode supports F31.2 (Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic) as a candidate. However, the subsequent two-week period of depressed mood meets criteria for a major depressive episode. Since the patient has experienced both a manic and a major depressive episode, this supports a diagnosis of F31.3 (Bipolar I disorder, current episode depressed). Both codes remain under consideration depending on the current focus of the episode and longitudinal course.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experienced additional symptoms of elevated mood, such as increased goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation, during the two-week period of high or irritable mood.
doctor.question: During that two-week period when you felt so high and irritable, did you find yourself doing things much more quickly or intensely than usual, like rushing around the shop constantly or working at a speed that was hard to keep up with?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I couldn’t sit still at the bench; I’d bounce from sketching a new watch case to emailing suppliers to rearranging display trays long after closing.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about increased activity, rushing around, and doing things quickly or intensely, which maps directly to the symptom of abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. It was like I had a motor running inside me that just wouldn't shut off, and the gas pedal was glued to the floor. I mean, usually, jewelry work is all about patience, right? It's a very stationary job. You sit at your bench, you get your loupe on your eye, you brace your arms, and you breathe slow so your hands stay perfectly steady. It's very focused. 

But during those two weeks? I literally couldn't sit still at the bench. I physically could not do it. I would sit down, grab my pencil, and I'd bounce from sketching this crazy new watch case—which, by the way, I don't even normally do watches, I'm mostly rings and pendants, but suddenly I was obsessed with this exposed-gear, rose-gold mechanical watch casing concept. I had all these ideas for the bezel and the lugs, just drawing furiously. But then, before I even finished the sketch, I’d just pop up out of my chair like I was on springs. 

I'd run over to the computer in the back office—well, it's really more of a storage closet with a laptop on a filing cabinet—and I'd start rapid-fire emailing all my suppliers. I'm talking metal brokers in New York, gemstone dealers, just demanding bulk quotes for all these materials I didn't even have the money for yet. And then, right in the middle of typing an email to a diamond guy, I'd suddenly decide the front showroom wasn't visually striking enough. So I'd leave the laptop open, march out to the front, and start completely rearranging all the velvet display trays. I'd pull every single piece out, color-coordinate the sapphires and the rubies, angle the rings so the track lighting hit the facets perfectly... 

And I'd be doing all of this long after closing time. The "Closed" sign had been flipped for hours, the street outside would be completely dead, pitch black, and I'm just in there pacing and bouncing from the bench to the computer to the display cases, over and over again, moving at warp speed. I was just a blur. It felt like if I stopped moving or working for even a single second, I’d just explode out of my own skin.

inference.note: The patient reported a distinct period of depressed mood following the manic episode, meeting criteria for a major depressive episode. This, combined with the prior manic episode, supports a diagnosis of Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, severe with psychotic features (F31.3). No other candidates remain.
